title: Build a mentoring practice that lasts beyond the first conversation
description: A sustainable plan for mentoring ten people: choose a format, set clear boundaries, follow through consistently and close relationships responsibly.
intent: How can I support ten people over time without treating them as a quota? This guide turns the milestone into a capacity-based mentoring practice. Design a manageable mentoring program for multiple people without treating mentees as a quota; focus on capacity and continuity.

sections.heading: Start with a role you can keep
paragraphs: Write down how much time you can reliably give in an ordinary month, including preparation and travel. Ten simultaneous weekly commitments may be less useful than a smaller active group plus a waitlist. Decide whether you mean one-to-one mentoring, group sessions, peer support or a time-limited skill project; those formats ask for different levels of continuity.

If you want to work with young people, approach established programs and ask about the screening, training, safeguarding rules and supervision they provide. MENTOR advises prospective mentors to compare organizations and discuss their availability and preferred format with coordinators. An informal professional conversation is not interchangeable with a youth program’s trained role.

sections.heading: Define a useful first goal
paragraphs: A first meeting should establish what the other person wants from the relationship. Ask what they are trying to learn, what kind of support is welcome and what a helpful next step would look like. Avoid arriving with a preselected life plan. A mentee may need practice explaining an idea, reviewing options or simply having a dependable listener.

Translate a broad aspiration into a small experiment. Instead of promising to “fix a career,” agree to review two project portfolios, rehearse one interview or identify questions for an advisor. Let the mentee own the decision. At the next meeting, revisit whether the experiment helped and change course if it did not.

sections.heading: Create continuity without overbooking
paragraphs: Use a simple private record of agreed actions, dates and preferences, while avoiding sensitive details the mentee has not asked you to retain. Set the next meeting before ending the current one. If you cannot meet for a period, say so early and offer a clear date for reconnecting rather than disappearing into an open-ended promise.

For a group, rotate attention deliberately: each person gets room to speak, and advice is offered only when requested. Do not compare progress or identify a “best” mentee. Keep the shared agenda practical, such as each person naming one obstacle and one small action. Offer individual follow-up where the program permits it.

sections.heading: Know the limits and use support
paragraphs: A mentor is a supportive relationship, not a substitute for counseling, medical care, legal advice or a program’s safeguarding staff. MENTOR specifically says mentors should refer serious concerns to appropriate professionals and contact the program coordinator about emergencies. Ask the organization beforehand how to escalate a safety concern and follow its local reporting rules.

Boundaries protect the relationship: agree on appropriate channels and hours, follow program guidance about gifts and transportation, and keep private disclosures confidential only within the limits the program explains. If you are matched through an organization, do not promise secrecy that conflicts with its safeguarding process. Clarify expectations in the first meeting.

sections.heading: Measure reliability, then close well
paragraphs: Track what you can control: whether you arrive, listen, keep agreements and help the mentee explore their own options. Do not score success by whether someone chooses your advice or reaches a milestone on your timetable. Invite periodic feedback with a concrete question such as, “Which part of these meetings should change?”

Ten meaningful relationships may accumulate across several years and different formats. When circumstances force an ending, contact the coordinator promptly and plan a respectful transition; MENTOR warns that abrupt withdrawal after trust is built can be harmful. A closeout can recap skills practiced, name ongoing supports and give the other person a genuine chance to say goodbye.

sources.title: Become a Mentor
sources.purpose: MENTOR recommends choosing a realistic time commitment, comparing programs, asking about matching, training and screening, and coordinating responsibly if a relationship must end.
